title: Morgan Stanley CEO James Gorman on trade, the Fed and more
description: Morgan Stanley chairman and CEO James Gorman joins CNBC's Wilfred Frost to discuss the impact of trade tensions on the global economy, the U.S. and its economic strength, the Fed and more.

asr.full_text: So we're here at your fourth annual senior multicultural leaders conference, tell us a little bit about what the day is and and what you hope to achieve. Well it's an idea, Carla Harris who is on the squawk. This morning, I really thought up brought this up. Four years ago and it's to bring together multicultural leaders but very senior C-sweet to talk about other ideas, network, great opportunities. Look for investment opportunities and we bring a bunch of Morgan Stanley's research, markets-based people together with a lot of outside executives. It's been a home run. She's done an unbelievable job. As you said, Carla was on Squawk Box this morning. I was interested that she said this is the fourth year and every single year has been sold out with a big waiting list. Yeah. I mean, to what extent does that show how keen people are to find better opportunities, to address some of the headwinds that some minorities face, and the lack of opportunities they have to address it? IMEISTER RICHARD BRANSON- I mean, it's endless right now. There's tremendous, tremendous demand. And unfortunately, there just aren't many opportunities to showcase. And this is one of them. I don't know if Carla mentioned, but she set up a venture lab where multicultural firms, start-ups can come and be part of Morgantown for a summer period. We provide them with all sorts of resources a little bit of financing, and then they go off and we present them to the marketplace. We have ten firms coming through this summer. They had 300 applications for it. Are you content with the level of diversity you have at the top of Morgan Sandler? I mean, when are you content? You're content when your organisation reflects the society you're in and it doesn't yet. But we've made strides. I mean we have a really diverse team relative to ten years ago when we started. We've got, this year, I think 28% of our managing directors were women. We've now got over 20% of the whole firm managing directors are women. When we started a few years ago, it was around 15%. So we've made strides. But listen, there's more to do. And what Carla's doing, what the team's doing here, is just a great initiative to say Morgan Stanley's really serious about this. I want to move on, James, and talk a little bit about the macroeconomic outlook. G20s just kicked off, as you know. How important is it that the U.S. and China don't escalate trade tensions further from where they are already over this weekend? I thought you were going to ask me how come Australia beat England in the World Cup. But I guess not. Well, I'd be at the spike losing I'd be happy to talk about the cricket World Cup at length. But I know I'd be fired if I did that. So we should talk about U.S. and China instead? Exactly. Just talk about U.S. and China. Listen and China instead? Let's talk about US and China. Listen, I was just in China a couple of weeks ago and I was in a meeting with Lighthizer in DC a week or two before that. We need a solution to this. There have been some trade disparities between the countries, but the US and China account for over 40% of global GDP. Nominal GDP is about $70 trillion. US and China combined are $30 trillion. We can't have a trade war. It will have a devastating effect to the global economy. That doesn't mean there can't be changes to the way the trade agreements are being written, and I think that's what the negotiators are figuring out. What did you learn from Ambassador Lighthizer? Do you think we're back to square one or are we close? This was, umm, let's see, probably 5 or 6 weeks ago. You know, it's a process, there's not going to be an arrival, that's like the kid in the backseat of the car, are we there yet? Are we there yet? Yet now we're here. No, it doesn't worth that way. This is going to go on these discussions I think for a decade. This is a resetting of a relationship with what is now the second-largest economy in the world. China's a 12 trillion dollar economy with all of its trading partners. So this is not something that's going to be solved by a meeting with the President Xi and President Trump of the G20 meeting. It's a resetting, there'll be many steps, and I think everybody understands that. Is it fair to say there is a relativelyS. economy has been relatively resilient so far in the face of that and do you expect that to continue? The economy has been resilient. The markets have been much more fragile, you know, the markets don't do well with uncertainty and this is a cloud of uncertainty so yeah the economy is resilient for good reason. The U.S. economy, you know, maybe I'm an outlier on this but the US economy is actually in pretty good shape. The U.S. economy, maybe I'm an outlier on this, but the U.S. economy is actually in pretty good shape. You have unemployment under 3 percent, under 4 percent. You've had increasing worker participation in the workforce. There's very modest inflation. All the states and municipalities that were supposed to be in financial trouble a decade ago, it didn't turn out that way. The U.S. economy is doing fine. This could derail it, It that hasn't yet. Given the relative strength of US economy, are you surprised at the level of the pivots we have seen from the Federal Reserve over the last six months? Highs in December and rhetoric we have had since then The Fed has in a tough place because the Fed's in a tough place, because the Fed's job obviously is safety and soundness and, overall, monetary stability. You know, when uncertainties rise to a big enough level, it does, in fact, affect how consumers behave. It does affect how corporate CEOs invest behind their companies. And when that is going on with this level of uncertainty, if you see it slowing, the question for the Fed is when do I preempt now my personal view is you be very aggressive on the way up in raising rates so that you you know you're stopping what could be an asset bubble at some point I personally would be more conservative in cutting rates because I don't think you want to use your fire power too early so the Fed is in a difficult position they They've got a bit of firepower, not much. I know they're going to have to use some. My guess is it looks like the market is pricing a rate cut next month, but they've got to be careful here. The economy is not weak yet. The uncertainties hovering over the economy are profound and that's the tension. The president's wrong to be calling for 50 basis points cuts right away. I'd never call the president wrong. What I would say Is that everybody has an opinion when you intervene. Right now if you read the fed language from the last fomc meeting It's suggestive that they prepared to move to a cut at 25 or 50 I'm not smart enough to know what the right answer is. Want to move a bit some Morgan Stanley-specific stuff and a slew of IPOs over the course of last quarter. Can that continue for the rest of this year, the pace we've seen in Q2? Oh, there are a lot of great companies out there that are lined up and, as we've seen, a lot of them are a late cycle, they've had multi-fundraisings. So that's, that's more challenging because investors are getting in the current round and getting in relatively late. There are a lot of tech deals still in the cycle, a lot of biotech deals. You guys led the Uber IPO. Did your bankers get the pricing wrong on that? What's wrong? Day one, the first five minutes, a month, we had the same issue with Facebook. I think on your show and I said, give it time. This is a great company. We're focused on how we trade in the market on that given day versus what the actual company is. And it was a tough week. I mean, the China trade stuff was going on. Now I think Uber was price fine and Uber is going to be fine. It's a great company. So on the Lyft IPO, CNBC Leslie Picker reported that you'd created some kind of synthetic short to help certain shareholders get around the lockup period they were in. Has that reporting made it harder for your ECM business to win further business? Well, firstly, there's a difference between reporting and facts. So we didn't have any problem with, and the allegations around that were ridiculous, frankly. So there was no synthetic shorts created whatsoever? No, we weren't creating shorts. We weren't trying to help people who shouldn't have been in a position where they could sell the stock. That's not what we did. And just to round off on the markets for the first portion of the interview, you mentioned that they'd been quite scared by the trade talk. When you look at all of the challenges out there at the moment, are you surprised to see markets at or near all-time highs? You know I've said this before, Wilfred, that if you think about a growing economy, increasing demographic population growth, by definition the market should finish at a high every single day. But it should be a surprise when they don't, logically. Now of course they don't because there are always these externalities. Which whips or back, you stand far enough back from an S&P chart and look over time, it's a straight line, bottom left corner, top, right, you get very, very close to it, and it's doing this. So am I surprised the market know, the US economy has been in phenomenal shape, let's just say that it's been in phenomenal shape. Am I surprised, there's now a lot of uncertainty about the future of that? No, not surprised about that either.
